reading.title: Why Flattery Can Fool Us
reading.purpose: Learn why praise can be used to trick people and how to protect yourself.
paras: Everyone likes to hear kind words, and that is why flattery can be so powerful. To flatter someone is to praise them too much, or not honestly, in order to win a favor. A person with a scheme, a secret and sly plan, may flatter someone so that the person stops thinking clearly.

Some people are easier to fool than others. A vain person is too proud of their looks or skills, and a conceited person thinks too highly of themselves. Both may enjoy praise so much that they believe it right away. Someone who is gullible believes things too quickly, so a trickster can deceive them by telling them something false.

Notice how people talk about themselves, too. To boast is to talk with too much pride about what you have or can do. Someone who likes to gloat enjoys a win in a mean way, perhaps by laughing at the player who lost. Someone who wants to mock others copies or teases them to make them feel small.

A hypocrite says one thing but does the opposite. Imagine a student who tells everyone to be honest and then copies a friend's homework. People quickly stop trusting a hypocrite, because the words and actions do not match.

You can protect yourself from tricks. When someone praises you, ask what that person wants. Check the facts before you believe a big claim. Real friends give you kind words, and they give you honest ones too.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, to "flatter" someone means to
choices: make fun of the person by copying the way he or she talks
give the person a gift before the person has asked for one
tell the person a secret that nobody else is allowed to know
praise the person too much, or not honestly
qs.why: The text defines it: to flatter is "to praise them too much, or not honestly, in order to win a favor."

qs.q: Which sentence explains why people stop trusting a hypocrite?
choices: Imagine a student who tells everyone to be honest and then copies a friend's homework.
A hypocrite says one thing but does the opposite.
People quickly stop trusting a hypocrite, because the words and actions do not match.
Check the facts before you believe a big claim.
qs.why: This is the only sentence that gives a reason: what a hypocrite says and does do not match.

ev.text: People quickly stop trusting a hypocrite, because the words and actions do not match.

qs.q: Why might a vain person believe a flatterer so quickly?
choices: The praise matches what the person already likes to think.
The person has learned to doubt everything that others say.
The person has always checked every fact before agreeing.
The flatterer is usually someone the person has never met.
qs.why: A vain person is proud of their looks or skills, so praise about them feels true and is easy to accept.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Friends should never say anything kind to each other, even when it is true.
Praise can trick people, so think carefully before you believe it.
Only vain people and conceited people are ever fooled by a trick.
Everyone who boasts or gloats is also a hypocrite who deceives.
qs.why: The reading shows how flattery and other behavior can fool people, then ends with ways to protect yourself.

clues.text: to praise them too much, or not honestly
enjoys a win in a mean way
